stories.title: Google DeepMind unveils Genie 4, a real-time world model that generates sound, speech and realistic physics
paragraphs: Google DeepMind announced Genie 4 on Oct. 27, 2026, describing it as its new world model for real-time interactive simulation. In a blog post by Raia Hadsell, Diego Rivas and Hang Qi, the lab says Genie 4 is natively multimodal and can generate music, ambient noise and interactive dialogue at the same time as the world itself, making it DeepMind's first real-time world model to generate audio natively.

According to DeepMind, Genie 4 builds on the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while Gemini 3.8 Flash acts as a guiding agent that watches the scene as it is generated, breaks goals into steps and checks whether each step succeeded. Users navigate with standard keyboard controls and can type prompts to change the scene while it runs, such as altering the weather, moving the camera or adding a person or object. DeepMind says the model simulates physics such as aerodynamics and collisions, and that its biggest leap is in how it simulates people who move, react and speak.

DeepMind also showed Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4 working together on robotics research, with Argon breaking a task into steps that steer the simulation; its example simulates Apptronik's Apollo humanoid playing checkers. The lab says trusted testers in film, journalism, education, gaming and engineering have been using the model for tasks such as pre-visualizing scenes and turning a single archival photo into an explorable simulation.

DeepMind calls Genie 4 an early, experimental model and says visual details and object permanence can still drift over longer sessions, with complex physics, audio accuracy, legible text and long-term consistency still under research. It is rolling out as a research preview to trusted testers, with access coming to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and to early-access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. DeepMind says all video and audio Genie 4 generates carries its SynthID watermark.

stories.title: Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate, an icy world beyond Pluto called 2026 ED138
paragraphs: Scientists have found a distant, icy body orbiting beyond Pluto that may be added to the solar system's official list of dwarf planets, according to a University of Washington release published on Phys.org on Oct. 27, 2026. The object, provisionally named 2026 ED138, was spotted earlier this month in data from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. The results were presented at a press conference on Oct. 27 by Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics who first spotted the object, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team.

According to the release, initial measurements place ED138 among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune. If confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. "Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić said. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope."

Holman found the object on the evening of Oct. 13 by running Rubin data through a search code he developed with colleague Kevin Napier, which compares billions of detections of moving objects to find the ones that belong to the same body. Jurić then found 20 more Rubin observations going back to March 2026, and the team also spotted ED138 in archival images from other surveys going back to 2016, giving them more than 10 years of its orbit. The release says the object sits in a crowded region of sky near the plane of the Milky Way, which is likely why it went unnoticed until now.

ED138 is currently about 46 astronomical units from the sun, compared with Pluto's average distance of 40 au. Based on its distance, brightness and estimated surface reflectivity, the team estimates it is between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (370 and 930 miles) across, and the release notes that icy bodies this large are expected to be round, one of the requirements for a dwarf planet. Further observations are needed to measure its exact size and confirm that it is a dwarf planet. The discovery follows Rubin's announcement in April of more than 11,000 new asteroids, including roughly 380 new trans-Neptunian objects, before its Legacy Survey of Space and Time formally began in June 2026.

stories.title: Greenhouse gases hit new record highs in 2025, with carbon dioxide at 426.8 parts per million, WMO reports
paragraphs: Levels of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide in the atmosphere all reached record highs in 2025, according to the World Meteorological Organization's annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin, published Oct. 27, 2026 and reported by Phys.org. The bulletin puts the globally averaged surface concentration of CO2 at 426.8 parts per million, or 153% of the preindustrial level in 1750. WMO releases it ahead of the U.N. climate conference, COP 31, which meets in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9 to 20.

The bulletin measures how much gas builds up in the atmosphere, not yearly emissions. WMO reports that CO2 growth rates have tripled since the 1960s, from an average of 0.8 ppm a year to 2.4 ppm a year in 2011 to 2020, and that CO2 rose by 2.8 ppm from 2024 to 2025, above the decade average but slightly less than the surge of 2023 to 2024. WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said the smaller rise reflects land carbon sinks recovering and fewer fire emissions after the strong 2023 to 2024 El Niño, and that she expects concentrations to rise further in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and a developing powerful El Niño.

Methane averaged 1,948 parts per billion in 2025, or 267% of its 1750 level, and nitrous oxide reached 339.1 ppb, or 126%. Citing NOAA's Annual Greenhouse Gas Index, the report says the warming effect of long-lived greenhouse gases rose 56% from 1990 to 2025, with CO2 accounting for about 81% of that increase.

WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett said the past 11 years have been the warmest on record. The bulletin also flags two gases tied to the clean-energy transition: sulfur hexafluoride, used in electricity distribution, which has a lifetime of more than 1,000 years and rose by a record amount in 2025, and hydrogen, which is not itself a greenhouse gas but has an indirect warming effect and increased 5.3% between 2010 and 2024.

stories.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6.1 Terra, a cheaper mid-range model built for computer use and visual reasoning
paragraphs: OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Terra on Oct. 26, 2026, describing it as a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use with clearer, more natural writing. The company calls it a significant step up from GPT-5.6 Terra and says it is aimed at everyday workplace tasks, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.

According to OpenAI, at medium reasoning effort GPT-6.1 Terra scores 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra on Agents' Last Exam, a benchmark of professional computer-use tasks, at about one-third the cost, and performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at one-tenth its price per token. OpenAI also reports that on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at maximum reasoning effort the model solves 50.3% of coding tasks, more than double GPT-5.6 Terra's published 21.5%, and that on its internal benchmark of error-inducing prompts the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% to 16.7%. OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choice for the most complex coding tasks.

OpenAI says the model meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework and keeps the protections developed for GPT-6 Astra. GPT-6.1 Terra is available starting Oct. 26 to Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, and to developers through the API as gpt-6.1-terra, at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, which OpenAI says is 50% lower than GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

Writing about the release the same day, developer Simon Willison noted that OpenAI's announcement emphasized visual reasoning and computer use, and compared Terra's place in OpenAI's lineup to Sonnet's in Anthropic's: neither the cheapest nor the most expensive option. He quoted OpenAI's Ted Sanders, who said on Hacker News that Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use but much faster, and a bit worse on most other things.

stories.title: NASA ends its Swift space telescope mission after a private rescue attempt fails
paragraphs: NASA has officially ended the mission of its Swift space telescope, Space.com reported on Oct. 26, 2026, citing a NASA statement issued on Friday, Oct. 23. Swift gathered its last scientific data on Oct. 20, according to that update, and NASA said the telescope is expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere "in the next few weeks."

Swift launched in November 2004 to study gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the cosmos. It was designed to operate for two years but kept working for more than two decades. According to NASA figures reported by Space.com, it observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and more than 1,400 supernova explosions, also studied asteroids, comets and black holes, and carried out an all-sky survey in X-ray light. Its data has contributed to about 7,000 published scientific papers. The observatory was renamed the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory in 2018 after its first principal investigator.

Swift was falling back toward Earth because of atmospheric drag and has no thrusters able to counteract it. In September 2025, NASA awarded Arizona company Katalyst Space Technologies a $30 million contract to try a rescue. Katalyst built a refrigerator-sized spacecraft called LINK, meant to grab Swift with three robotic arms and boost it to a higher orbit. LINK launched on July 3, but about three weeks later it had problems with its propulsion system and reaction wheels that set it spinning at an unexpected rate. It got within about 12 to 15 kilometers (7.5 to 9.3 miles) of Swift and photographed it, but could not capture it, and LINK fell back to Earth on Sept. 25.

"Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe," said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA Headquarters. He called the rescue "a high-risk, high-reward mission" and said it was worthwhile for advancing U.S. spacecraft servicing technology. "Swift leaves us with an extraordinary archive of multiwavelength observations that will fuel new discoveries for decades more," he said in the Oct. 23 statement.

stories.title: Anthropic files to go public, with plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT
paragraphs: Anthropic announced on Oct. 26, 2026, that it has filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock. The company says it intends to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT," and that the number of shares to be offered and the price range have not yet been determined. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are named as the lead underwriters.

According to CNBC's coverage of the filing, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.29 billion for the six months ended June 30, 2026, up 1,304% from $1.16 billion a year earlier, and $4.59 billion in revenue for all of 2025. It reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of 2026, which the company says largely reflects accounting charges from changes in the value of convertible notes tied to increases in its valuation. CNBC reports that consumption-based revenue made up 80% of the total in that period and subscriptions 20%.

CNBC reports that the filing describes a governance structure Anthropic says has "no direct public company precedent." A company called Founder LLC, whose sole members are Anthropic's seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, will hold 50.1% of the voting power of outstanding shares. Anthropic says in the filing that the structure may make it more difficult to replace its directors and management and is likely to limit the chance of an unsolicited takeover.

CNBC reports the filing lists 5,300 employees as of Sept. 30, more than 11,900 enterprise customers with at least $100,000 in trailing-twelve-month revenue, and more than 90 pages of risk factors, including AI safety, dependence on TSMC for chips, and data center construction moratoriums. The filing names OpenAI and Google as its direct competitors and, according to CNBC, describes a compute agreement with SpaceX of up to $120.5 billion running into 2029. Anthropic says no sales can take place until the registration statement becomes effective.
